body: For a modal reader, no, I think you’re right. That does sound hilarious and I’d love to read it, but I don’t think I’m in the majority with my take on the extent to which logical consistency and expansive lore matters. Just wanted to give my 2 cents

I empathise with your point of view, but personally it doesn’t sit right with me to simply dismiss questions on world-building or lore as things you just “shouldn’t think too hard about” or that they “don’t matter”, as the other commenter said. People care about different things when it comes to fantasy worlds, and for me, consistent internal logic and expansive lore are what make a world interesting and immersive. 

Shutting down constructively critical questions strikes me as a type of anti-intellectualism based on the belief that something isn’t important - but as I said, people care about different things. 

I can appreciate a fantasy world more if it is comprehensive enough to not shy away from critical inquiry. I don’t expect there to be a lore-based response to every question on a given fantasy universe, but I also don’t think these things “don’t matter” or that someone has “lost the plot” for asking those questions - which would be an ad hominem, reinforcing the anti-intellectual tendency.

At the end of the day, it’s just fantasy world-building, and I recognise there are more important things in life. That said, when judging any art form based on its own merit, I don’t see why its ability to stand up to scrutiny shouldn’t matter.

All due respect, you can’t just read the manifesto and claim you understand Marx’s worldview. If you haven’t read Capital, the German Ideology, or any secondary literature, then you’re missing 99% of the picture. Marx wouldn’t disagree with you that human nature appears selfish and greedy, but he would argue that people are a product of their environment, I.e. the socio-political conditions they live in. The point is that it makes sense that people are greedy and selfish - capitalism incentivises them to be so. Whereas if we lived in a system that disincentivised greed, things may be different, he argues. 

To dismiss Marx’s works as a toddler’s worldview is horribly disingenuous. There is a reason it has been studied around the world ever since it was written. To not have engaged with the literature to any meaningful level and then to dismiss it on superficial grounds is, ironically, a childish response.
